title: The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable

facts.claim: Calibration test described in the book: people give a range they are 98 percent confident contains the answer (e.g. population of Rajasthan); about 2 percent should miss. Researchers found the miss rate close to 45 percent; the first sample was Harvard Business School students.

Philip Tetlock asked political and economic experts to judge the likelihood of events about five years ahead: around 27,000 predictions from close to 300 specialists, about a quarter economists. Error rates were many times what experts estimated; a PhD gave no edge over an undergraduate degree, well-published professors none over journalists; those with big reputations predicted worse.
Experts' defences Tetlock catalogued: 'I was playing a different game', 'it was an outlier', 'I was almost right'.

Taleb reviewed economics papers: no convincing evidence economists can predict; at best slightly better than random. Makridakis and Hibon's M-Competitions (M3 completed 1999): statistically sophisticated methods do not necessarily give more accurate forecasts than simpler ones.
Taleb's advice: invest in preparedness, not in prediction.

Turkey (after Bertrand Russell's chicken): fed every day, each feeding firms its belief that humans look after it; on the Wednesday afternoon before Thanksgiving it is slaughtered. Its sense of safety was highest when the risk was highest. Figure: 'One thousand and one days of history'.

Barbell strategy: rather than 'medium risk', put about 85-90 percent in extremely safe instruments like Treasury bills and 10-15 percent in extremely speculative bets; no Black Swan can hurt beyond the floor.

Positive vs negative Black Swan businesses: movies, some publishing, scientific research, venture capital lose small to win big; military, catastrophe insurance, banking and lending face mainly downside. William Goldman: 'Nobody knows anything' about movie sales.
Editorial caveat: Tetlock's later Good Judgment Project (Superforecasting, 2015) found some forecasters reliably beat chance on short horizons.
After the 45 percent result Taleb asks: 'Are we twenty-two times too comfortable with what we know? It seems so.' In Tetlock's sample economists were about a quarter.

Tetlock's main focus was less the experts' competence than why they did not realize they were not good at their own business: how they spun their stories afterwards (belief defense, protecting self-esteem).

rejected.claim: 'Expert forecasts were not significantly different from random guessing'
rejected.reason: Taleb says economists' predictions are at best slightly better than random; Tetlock's finding is about error rates and reputation

'Antifragile' as a concept of The Black Swan
rejected.reason: Term and framework come from Taleb's later book Antifragile (2012)

rejected.claim: 'Manage small losses to build immunity to large shocks' as Black Swan advice
rejected.reason: Immunity framing is Antifragile; Black Swan's version is the barbell and limiting downside
